blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Electric Current :

• Rate of flow of charge through cross-section of a conductor is called electric current.
    • If a charge $\Delta$Q crosses an area in time ∆t then the average electric current through the area, during this time is

$\mathrm{i}_{\mathrm{av}}=\dfrac{\Delta \mathrm{Q}}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}=\dfrac{\text { Average charge flow }}{\text { time taken }}=\dfrac{\text { ne }}{\mathrm{t}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{C}}{\mathrm{~s}}=\text { Ampere }$

Classification of Current :

Some important points about current :

(1) Current is a fundamental quantity with dimensions$\left[\mathrm{M}^0 \mathrm{~L}^0 \mathrm{~T}^0 \mathrm{~A}^1\right]$

(2) Current is a scalar quantity with its SI unit being ampere and it does not follow vector law of addition.

(3) Direction of current is in the direction of flow of positive charge or we can say opposite to the direction of flow of negative charge.

(4) Slope of q – t graph gives us current.

(5) Area under i-t curve gives us total charge flown.

modules.name: Mean Free Path, Drift Velocity and Current Density

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Behaviour of conductor on applying potential difference across it at room temperature

• Before application of electric field between ends of conductor, Path is straight line between two successive collisions.
    • After application of electric field between ends of conductor, Path is curved between two successive collisions.
Mean Relaxation Time (τ): The time taken by free electrons between two successive collision is called relaxation time (t) and average of all these times is called mean relaxation time.

$\tau=\dfrac{\tau_1+\tau_2+\tau_3+\ldots \ldots \tau_N}{N} \text { (Order of } \tau=10^{-14} \mathrm{sec} \text {.) }$

Drift Velocity: Due to application of potential difference across conductor an electric field is produced inside the conductor. Due to electric field, free electron experience force opposite to the direction of electric field. Due to this force these electrons start drifting in the opposite direction of electric field and during motion they face many collision with heavy positive ions in their path. So the velocity with which e– effectively displaced is called drift velocity.

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{V}}_{\mathrm{d}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{e} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \tau}{\mathrm{~m}}$

Note: This drift velocity is very low of order $10^{-4} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$  but electrical appliances immediately starts working just after switch is on because electric field propagates with the speed of light in circuit and instantly exert the force on free electron at their own location.

Important points about current carrying conductor

• All free e– moves with $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{d}}$ (drift velocity).

• There is no accumulation of charge in current carrying conductor. This implies charges entering at one end of conductor is equal to the charges leaving from the other end.

Relation between drift velocity and current :

$\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{neAV}_d$

Current density (J) :

• It is defined as current flowing per unit cross-sectional area of conductor.
    • It gives us information about magnitude & direction of current passing through an area.
    • Current density is a vector quantity having direction of electric field or direction of current flow, from definition of current density.

$(J)=\dfrac{I}{Acos\theta}$

$\mathrm{I}=(\mathrm{J}) A \cos \theta$

$\mathrm{I}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{J}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~A}}$

For non-uniform distribution of current :

$\text { current density }(\mathrm{J})=\frac{\mathrm{dI}}{\mathrm{dA} \cos \theta}$

$d I=J(d A \cos \theta) \text { or } \quad \mathrm{I}=\int \mathrm{J}(\mathrm{~d} A \cos \theta)$

Relation between current density & electric field :

$\mathrm{J}=\mathrm{ne} \dfrac{\mathrm{eE} \tau}{\mathrm{~m}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{ne}^2 \mathrm{E} \tau}{\mathrm{~m}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{ne}^2 \mathrm{E} \tau}{\mathrm{~m}}=\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{ne}^2 \tau}{\mathrm{~m}}\right) \mathrm{E}  \text { or }  \mathrm{J}=\sigma \mathrm{E}$

Mobility $(\boldsymbol{\mu})$: Ease of movement of charge carriers within a conductor known as mobility of charge carriers.

• It is defined as drift velocity per unit electric field

$\mu=\dfrac{v_d}{E}=\dfrac{1}{E} \dfrac{e E \tau}{m} \Rightarrow \mu=\dfrac{e \tau}{m}$

Note: On increasing temperature of conductor, frequency of collision increases and hence average relaxation time decreases.

$\text{temperature} \uparrow, \tau \downarrow$

$v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}, \quad V_d \downarrow$

$\sigma = \dfrac{ne^2 \tau}{m}, \quad \sigma \downarrow, \quad \rho \uparrow$

$\mu = \dfrac{e \tau}{m}, \quad \mu \downarrow$

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Ohm’s Law: If physical quantities like temperature, pressure, volume, length, cross-section or nature of the material kept constant then current through a conductor is directly proportional to potential difference applied across it. This is called Ohm’s law.

$\begin{aligned} & V \propto I \quad[\text { Ohm's law }] \\ & \frac{V}{I}=\text { constant }=\mathrm{R}(\text { Resistance }) \end{aligned}$

V-I characteristics: At constant temperature, current is directly proportional to the applied potential difference. This law is called ohm's law and substances which obey it are called ohmic or linear conductors.

Effect of Stretching on Resistance of Wire

$\mathrm{R} \propto \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{~A}^2} \propto \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{r}^4} \propto \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{D}^4}$

$\text { On stretching: } \ell \uparrow, \quad A \downarrow, \quad R \uparrow$

Resistivity : The resistivity (specific resistance) of a material is equal to the resistance of a wire of that material with unit cross sectional area and unit length.

$\rho=\left(\dfrac{m_e}{n e^2 \tau}\right)$

$\text { S.I. unit of resistivity is }=\Omega \mathrm{m} \text {. }$

$\text { Conductivity is the inverse of resistivity } \sigma=\frac{1}{\rho}$

$\text { Where } \sigma=\frac{\mathrm{ne}^2 \tau}{\mathrm{~m}} \text { is Conductivity of a material }$

Conductivity is degree to which a material conducts electricity.

$\text { Resistivity }(\rho) \text { and conductivity }(\sigma) \text { depends on : }$

(1) Nature of material

(2) Temperature of material

Resistivity and conductivity does not depend on the size and shape of the material because it is a characteristic property of the conducting material.

Temperature Dependence of Resistivity and Resistance :

$\rho_{\mathrm{T}}=\rho_0\left[1+\alpha\left(T-T_0\right)\right]$

$\text { Unit of } \alpha \text { is } \frac{1}{{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}}$

Resistance  :

$\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{T}}=\mathrm{R}_0(1+\alpha \Delta \mathrm{T})$

$\alpha$ is called the temperature co-efficient of resistivity.

For metals : $\alpha$ is positive

For semiconductors and insulators : $\alpha$ is negative

Series Combination:

$\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{eq}}=\mathrm{R}_1+\mathrm{R}_2+\mathrm{R}_3$

Note:

(a)$\text { In series, I } \rightarrow \text { same }$

(b)$\text { Since } I \text { is same; } V \propto R \text { (As } V=I R)$

(c) For n identical resistances in series:

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{eq}}=\mathrm{nR} \\ & \mathrm{~V}_1=\mathrm{V}_2=\mathrm{V}_3=\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{n}}=\frac{\mathrm{V}_{\text {battery }}}{\mathrm{n}} \end{aligned}$

(d) $\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{eq}}>\left(\mathbf{R}_{\max }\right)_{\text {combination }}$

Parallel Combination :

$\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{eq}}}=\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}_1}+\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}_2}+\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}_3}$

Note:

(a) In parallel V is same across all resistors but current will be different.

(b)$\text { Since } V \text { is same, } I \propto \frac{1}{R}$

(c) In case of 2 resistance  $\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}}=\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}_1}+\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}_2} \Rightarrow \mathrm{R}=\dfrac{\mathrm{R}_1 \mathrm{R}_2}{\mathrm{R}_1+\mathrm{R}_2}$

(d) If n equal resistance are connected in parallel

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{eq}}=\mathrm{R} / \mathrm{n} \\ & \mathrm{I}_1=\mathrm{I}_2=\mathrm{I}_3=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{n}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{total}}}{\mathrm{n}} \end{aligned}$

(e) $\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{eq}}<\left(\mathbf{R}_{\min }\right)_{\text {combination }}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Kirchhoff’s First law : This law is also known as junction law or current law (KCL). According to it- In an electric circuit, the algebraic sum of the currents meeting at any junction in the circuit is zero.

Sum of the currents entering the junction is equal to sum of the currents leaving the junction.

This is based on law of conservation of charge.

$\mathrm{i}_1-\mathrm{i}_2-\mathrm{i}_3-\mathrm{i}_4+\mathrm{i}_5=0$

$\mathrm{i}_1+\mathrm{i}_5=\mathrm{i}_2+\mathrm{i}_3+\mathrm{i}_4$

Kirchhoff’s Second law : This law is also known as loop rule or voltage law (KVL) and according to it in any closed circuit the algebraic sum of e.m.f. and algebraic sum of potential drops is zero.

$\Sigma \mathrm{IR}+\Sigma \mathrm{E}=0 .$

In the following closed loop,

$-\mathrm{i}_1 \mathrm{R}_1-\mathrm{i}_1 \mathrm{R}_2-\mathrm{E}_1-\mathrm{i}_4 \mathrm{R}_3+\mathrm{E}_2+\mathrm{E}_3+\mathrm{i}_4 \mathrm{R}_4=0$

Sign Convention for the Applications of Kirchhoff's Second Law

For the application of Kirchhoff's laws, the following sign conventions are to be considered.

• The change in potential in traversing a resistance in the direction of the current is -iR, while in the opposite direction, it is +iR.

Mirror Symmetry

(1) It is applied along perpendicular bisector of line AB (A and B are the points about which Req. is to be calculated).

(2) We can remove resistances and junctions which are on the line of symmetry.

(3) Points on line of symmetry are equipotential points.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Basic Definitions associated with cells and batteries

Symbol of a Cell :

1. EMF(Electromotive Force)(E) : The voltage across the terminals of a cell when it is not delivering any current is called EMF of the cell.

2.Internal Resistance of a Cell(r) : Resistance offered by the electrolyte of the cell when an electric current flows through it is known as internal resistance.

Dependency of internal resistance r is :

  • distance between two electrodes increases$\rightarrow$ r increases
  • Area dipped in electrolyte increases $\rightarrow$r decreases
  • Concentration of electrolyte increases  $\rightarrow$r increases
  • Temperature increases  $\rightarrow$ r decreases
3. Terminal Potential Difference(V) :

• When current is drawn through a cell or current is supplied to it then the potential difference across its terminals is called terminal voltage.

1. During Discharging of a Cell :

The current flows inside the cell from the cathode to the anode.

Current,

$I=\dfrac{E}{R+r}$

$\begin{aligned}
& V_A-E+I r=V_B \\
& V_A-V_B=E-I r
\end{aligned}$

$V=E-I r$

2. When Cell is getting Charged :

Current inside the cell is from anode to cathode.

Current, $I=\dfrac{V-E}{r}$

$\begin{aligned}
& V_A-E+I r=V_B \\
& V_A-V_B=E-I r
\end{aligned}$

During charging the terminal potential difference is greater than the emf of the cell

3. When cell is short circuited :

In short Circuit  $R=0$

$I=\dfrac{E}{R+r}=\dfrac{E}{r} \text { and } V=I R=0$

Note: In short circuit, current from the cell is maximum and terminal potential difference is zero

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Combination of cells in Series and in Parallel

A. Series Combination : When cells are connected in series the total emf of the series combination is equal to the sum of the emf's of the individual cells and the internal resistance of the cells will also be in series.

$\begin{aligned} & E_{e q}=E_1+E_2+E_3+\cdots+E_n \\ & r_{\text {eq }}=r_1+r_2+r_3+\cdots+r_2 \end{aligned}$

B. Parallel Combination :

$\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{eq}}=\dfrac{\dfrac{\mathrm{E}_1}{\mathrm{r}_1}+\dfrac{\mathrm{E}_2}{\mathrm{r}_2}+\dfrac{\mathrm{E}_3}{\mathrm{r}_3}}{\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{r}_1}+\dfrac{1}{r_2}+\dfrac{1}{r_3} \ldots} $

$\quad \dfrac{1}{r_{e q}}=\dfrac{1}{r_1}+\dfrac{1}{r_2}+\dfrac{1}{r_3} \ldots$

When cell support each other

$\begin{aligned} & E_{e q}=\dfrac{E_1 r_2+E_2 r_1}{r_1+r_2} \\ & r_{e q}=\dfrac{r_1+r_2}{r_1+r_2} \end{aligned}$

When cells are connected with opposite polarity

$\begin{aligned} &\text { Let } \mathrm{E}_1>\mathrm{E}_2\\ &\begin{aligned} & E_{e q}=\frac{E_1 r_2-E_2 r_1}{r_1+r_2} \\ & r_{e q}=\frac{r_1 r_2}{r_1+r_2} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$

Note: If n identical cells are connected in parallel and then :-

$\begin{aligned} E_{e q} & =n \dfrac{E / r}{n / r} \\ E_{e q} & =E \\ r_{e q} & =\dfrac{r}{n} \end{aligned}$

Circuit Analysis Involving Combination of Cells

If n identical cells are connected in series and there are m such branches in the circuit then

Total number of cells in this circuit = nm

Internal resistance of the cells connected in a row = nr

total e.m.f. of the cells connected in a row = $E_{\text {net }}$ = nE

Since there are m such rows,

$\text { Total internal resistance of the circuit } \mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{net}}=\frac{\mathrm{nr}}{\mathrm{~m}}$

Total e.m.f. of the circuit = total e.m.f. of the cells connected in a row

$=\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{net}}=\mathrm{nE}$

$\text { Current in the circuit } \mathrm{I}=\dfrac{\mathrm{E}_{\text {net }}}{\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{r}_{\text {net }}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{nE}}{\mathrm{R}+\dfrac{\mathrm{nr}}{\mathrm{~m}}}$

Note : Current I in the circuit is maximum when external resistance in the circuit is equal to the total internal resistance of the cells.

Special case: If in a battery of n identical cells, m cells are wrongly connected. (Consider them is series)

$\text { Number of cells supporting }=(\mathrm{n}-\mathrm{m})$

$\text { Total emf of such cells }=(n-m) E$

$\text { Total emf of cells opposing }=\mathrm{mE}$

$\text { Resultant emf of battery }=(n-m) E-m E=(n-2 m) E$

$\text { Total internal resistance of cells }=\mathrm{nr}$

$\left.\mathrm{E}_{\text {net }}=(\mathrm{n}-2 \mathrm{~m}) \mathrm{E} \quad \text { (Condition } \quad \mathrm{n}>2 \mathrm{~m}\right)$

$I_{n e t}=\dfrac{(n-2 m) E}{R+n r}$

blocks.text:
Wheatstone Bridge: It is used to find unknown resistance in circuit. None of the shown resistance are in series and none of them are in a parallel.

Balancing condition

$\text { If }\left\{\dfrac{R_1}{R_2}=\dfrac{R_3}{R_4}\right\} $, then bridge is said to be balanced, in this case:

$\begin{aligned} &\left[\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{x}}=\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{y}}\right]\\ &\text { Thus, no current flows in xy branch. } \end{aligned}$

$\dfrac{\mathrm{R}_1}{\mathrm{R}_2}=\dfrac{\mathrm{R}_3}{\mathrm{R}_4} \text { or } \mathrm{R}_1 \mathrm{R}_4=\mathrm{R}_2 \mathrm{R}_3$

Galvanometer : It is used to detect the current i.e. whether current is flowing or not and whether direction of current is reversed or not.

  • Its working is based on torque on current carrying coil. $(\theta \propto i)$
  • Measures small value of current.
  • Maximum value of current at which galvanometer shows maximum deflection or full scale deflection is known as$\text { ' } \mathrm{i}_{\mathrm{g}} \text { ' }$
$\text { Sensitivity = Response/input }$

$\text { (a) Current sensitivity }=\dfrac{\theta}{I}$

$\text { (b) Voltage sensitivity }=\dfrac{\theta}{\mathrm{v}}$

Ammeter:

An ammeter is connected in series with a current carrying wire to measure current passing through it. Since it is connected to the wire and has a finite amount of resistance, there will be some potential difference across it. This will lead to the change in actual flow of current. In an ideal situation where the ammeter can

measure the actual current passing through a wire, there should be no voltage drop across it and hence its resistance should be zero.

Conversion of Galvanometer into Ammeter

• To convert a galvanometer into an ammeter a very small resistance is connected in parallel to the galvanometer called SHUNT.
    • Resistance of an ammeter is very small and it is zero for ideal ammeter i.e. ideal ammeter behaves like conducting wire.
    • Value of shunt.

$\Rightarrow \mathrm{S}=\left[\dfrac{\mathrm{i}_{\mathrm{g}}}{\mathrm{i}-\mathrm{i}_{\mathrm{g}}}\right] \mathrm{G} \Rightarrow \mathrm{~S}=\left[\dfrac{1}{\dfrac{\mathrm{i}}{\mathrm{i}_{\mathrm{g}}}-1}\right] \mathrm{G} \Rightarrow \mathrm{~S}=\left[\dfrac{\mathrm{G}}{\mathrm{n}-1}\right] \text { Where } \mathrm{n}=\dfrac{\mathrm{i}}{\mathrm{i}_{\mathrm{g}}}$

$\text { Where, G - resistance of galvanometer }$

$\mathbf{i}_{\mathrm{g}} $ - range of galvanometer or current required to produce full deflection.

i - Range of ammeter [Max. current can be measured.]$$

Voltmeter :

A voltmeter is connected in parallel to the current carrying wire, to measure the potential difference between two points. Since it is connected to the wire, a finite amount of current will pass through it. This will lead to the change in actual flow of current and hence change in the actual potential difference. In an ideal situation where the voltmeter can measure the actual potential difference across two points, there should be no current passing through it and hence its resistance should be infinite.

Conversion of Galvanometer into Voltmeter:

1. To convert galvanometer into voltmeter, a high resistance is connect in series with a galvanometer.

2. Resistance of voltmeter is very high and it is infinite for ideal voltmeter. so ideal voltmeter ⎯→ open circuit

Resistance R and (G+H) are in parallel between points A and B so we can write

$\mathrm{H}=\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{v}-\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{g}}}{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{g}}}\right) \mathrm{G}=\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{g}}}-1\right) \mathrm{G}$

$\mathrm{H}=(\mathrm{n}-1) \mathrm{G} \quad \text { where } \mathrm{n}=\dfrac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{g}}}$

$\text { V: Range of voltmeter, } \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{g}} \text { : Range of galvanometer }$

Meter Bridge:

(1) It is used to find unknown resistance in circuit.

(2) Its working is based on Wheatstone Bridge principle.

MB circuit :

a. It has a wire of 1 m on which balancing point is to be search.

b. Resistance of copper-strips are negligible due to very low resistivity and greater cross- sectional area.

c. MB wire is taken of constantan or Manganin due negligible temperature co-efficient of resistance $\alpha$. So resistance of the wire doesn’t change during the experiment.

Working : Initially a resistance R is taken out from a resistance box and jockey is tapped on the wire. Find balancing point B where deflection in galvanometer becomes zero. Distance of this point B from left end (A) is called balancing length $'l'$.

Balancing condition

$\dfrac{P}{Q}=\dfrac{R}{S} \Rightarrow \dfrac{R}{\rho \ell / A}=\dfrac{S}{\dfrac{\rho(100-\ell)}{A}} \Rightarrow S=\left[\dfrac{100-\ell}{\ell}\right] R$

• Balancing length is independent of the radius of the cross-section of the wire.
    • Jockey should not be rubbed against the wire because rubbing action changes the cross-section of the wire.
    • END ERROR and END CORRECTION – this error occurs due to neglecting resistances at the connection point A & C. End corrections  $e_1 \& e_2$  are the lengths corresponding to resistances at connection points so equation becomes.

$\dfrac{\ell+\mathrm{e}_1}{(100-\ell)+\mathrm{e}_2}=\dfrac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{~S}}$

Cause of Heating: When current passes through the conductor then drifting electrons transfer their energy to atoms in collisions which increases thermal energy of the conductor, results in increase in temperature. Energy is lost in surroundings in form of heat.

$\mathrm{H}=\mathrm{i}^2 \mathrm{Rt}=\dfrac{\mathrm{V}^2}{\mathrm{R}}=\mathrm{Vit}$

SI unit : joule

Practical Units : 1 kilowatt hour (kWh)

$1 \mathrm{kWh}=3.6 \times 10^6 \text { joules }=1 \text { unit }$

Maximum power transfer theorem

$\text { (a) } P=i^2 R=\left[\dfrac{E}{R+r}\right]^2 R$

If P = max

$\text { Then } \dfrac{\mathrm{dP}}{\mathrm{dR}}=0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{\mathrm{~d}}{\mathrm{dR}}\left[\left[\dfrac{\mathrm{E}}{\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{r}}\right]^2 \mathrm{R}\right]=0$

On solving R = r So, to deliver maximum power to the load resistance. Load resistance should be equal to internal resistance of the cell.

$\text { (b) } i_{P(\max )}=\dfrac{E}{R+R}=\dfrac{E}{2 R}=\dfrac{E}{2 r}$

$\text { where } i_{\mathrm{p}_{(\max )}}=\text { current in case of max. power delivered. }$

$\begin{aligned} & \text { (c) } P_{(\max )}=\left[\frac{E}{2 R}\right]^2 R \\ & P_{(\max )}=\frac{E^2}{4 R}=\frac{E^2}{4 r} \end{aligned}$

Resistance of an electrical device

$\begin{aligned} & R=\frac{V_S^2}{P_S}=\frac{V_A^2}{P_C} \Rightarrow \frac{V_S^2}{P_S}=\frac{V_A^2}{P_C} \\ & \text { Hence } P_C=\left(\frac{V_A}{V_S}\right) P_S \end{aligned}$

$\text { As } \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{s}}=\text { constant } \Rightarrow \mathrm{R} \propto \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{s}}}$

$P_S \uparrow, R \downarrow \text {, thickness of filament } \uparrow$

$\text { For example : } \mathrm{R}_{40 \mathrm{~W}}>\mathrm{R}_{100 \mathrm{W}}$

Combination of bulbs

(a) Series combination

$\begin{aligned} & R=R_1+R_2 \\ & \frac{V^2}{P}=\frac{V_1^2}{P_1}+\frac{V_2^2}{P_2} \end{aligned}$

(When rated voltage is not given, take it equal to applied voltage.)

$\begin{aligned} &\frac{1}{\mathrm{P}}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{P}_1}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{P}_2}\\ &\text { In case of } \mathrm{n} \text {-identical bulbs }\\ &P_{\text {series }}=\frac{P}{n} \end{aligned}$

Note:

$\text { Brightness } \propto \text { Power consumed by bulb } \propto \mathrm{R} \propto \frac{1}{\mathrm{P}_{\text {rated }}} \text {. }$

Bulb of lesser wattage will shine more.

$\text { For same current } P=I^2 R \quad \text { so } \quad P \propto R \Rightarrow R \uparrow, P \uparrow$

(b) Parallel combination

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{R}=\frac{1}{R_1}+\frac{1}{R_2} \\ & \frac{P}{V_S^2}=\frac{P_1}{V_s^2}+\frac{P_2}{V_S^2} \\ & P=P_1+P_2 \end{aligned}$

In case of n-identical bulbs

$\mathrm{P}_{\text {parallel }}=\mathrm{nP}$

Note:

Brightness $ \propto \text { power consumed by bulb } \propto \frac{1}{\mathrm{R}} \propto \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{s}}$

Bulb of greater wattage will shine more.

For same V,  P = $\frac{\mathrm{V}^2}{\mathrm{R}} $  more power will be consumed in smaller resistance P $\propto$ $\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}}$

Let two coil boil some amount of water in times  $\mathrm{t}_1 \text { and } \mathrm{t}_2$ separately Now these coils are connected in series and then parallel then time required to boil same amount of water.

In series combination

$\begin{aligned} &\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{\mathrm{P}}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{P}_1}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{P}_2} \\ & \frac{\mathrm{t}}{\mathrm{H}}=\frac{\mathrm{t}_1}{\mathrm{H}}+\frac{\mathrm{t}_2}{\mathrm{H}} \end{aligned}\\ &\mathrm{t}=\mathrm{t}_1+\mathrm{t}_2 \end{aligned}$

In parallel combination

$\begin{aligned} & P=P_1+P_2 \\ & \frac{H}{t}=\frac{H}{t_1}+\frac{H}{t_2} \\ & \frac{1}{t}=\frac{1}{t_1}+\frac{1}{t_2} \Rightarrow t=\frac{t_1 t_2}{t_1+t_2} \end{aligned}$

NOTE: Instruments based on heating effects of current, work with both A.C. and D.C. Equal values of A.C. (RMS) and D.C. produce equal heating effect. Due to this reason, the brightness of bulb is same whether it is operated by A.C. or an equivalent D.C.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Behaviour of conductor on applying potential difference across it at room temperature

• Before application of electric field between ends of conductor, Path is straight line between two successive collisions.
    • After application of electric field between ends of conductor, Path is curved between two successive collisions.
Mean Relaxation Time (τ): The time taken by free electrons between two successive collision is called relaxation time (t) and average of all these times is called mean relaxation time.

$\tau=\dfrac{\tau_1+\tau_2+\tau_3+\ldots \ldots \tau_N}{N} \text { (Order of } \tau=10^{-14} \mathrm{sec} \text {.) }$

Drift Velocity: Due to application of potential difference across conductor an electric field is produced inside the conductor. Due to electric field, free electron experience force opposite to the direction of electric field. Due to this force these electrons start drifting in the opposite direction of electric field and during motion they face many collision with heavy positive ions in their path. So the velocity with which e– effectively displaced is called drift velocity.

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{V}}_{\mathrm{d}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{e} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \tau}{\mathrm{~m}}$

Note: This drift velocity is very low of order $10^{-4} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$  but electrical appliances immediately starts working just after switch is on because electric field propagates with the speed of light in circuit and instantly exert the force on free electron at their own location.

Important points about current carrying conductor

• All free e– moves with $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{d}}$ (drift velocity).

• There is no accumulation of charge in current carrying conductor. This implies charges entering at one end of conductor is equal to the charges leaving from the other end.

Relation between drift velocity and current :

$\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{neAV}_d$

Current density (J) :

• It is defined as current flowing per unit cross-sectional area of conductor.
    • It gives us information about magnitude & direction of current passing through an area.
    • Current density is a vector quantity having direction of electric field or direction of current flow, from definition of current density.

$(J)=\dfrac{I}{Acos\theta}$

$\mathrm{I}=(\mathrm{J}) A \cos \theta$

$\mathrm{I}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{J}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~A}}$

For non-uniform distribution of current :

$\text { current density }(\mathrm{J})=\frac{\mathrm{dI}}{\mathrm{dA} \cos \theta}$

$d I=J(d A \cos \theta) \text { or } \quad \mathrm{I}=\int \mathrm{J}(\mathrm{~d} A \cos \theta)$

Relation between current density & electric field :

$\mathrm{J}=\mathrm{ne} \dfrac{\mathrm{eE} \tau}{\mathrm{~m}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{ne}^2 \mathrm{E} \tau}{\mathrm{~m}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{ne}^2 \mathrm{E} \tau}{\mathrm{~m}}=\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{ne}^2 \tau}{\mathrm{~m}}\right) \mathrm{E}  \text { or }  \mathrm{J}=\sigma \mathrm{E}$

Mobility $(\boldsymbol{\mu})$: Ease of movement of charge carriers within a conductor known as mobility of charge carriers.

• It is defined as drift velocity per unit electric field

$\mu=\dfrac{v_d}{E}=\dfrac{1}{E} \dfrac{e E \tau}{m} \Rightarrow \mu=\dfrac{e \tau}{m}$

Note: On increasing temperature of conductor, frequency of collision increases and hence average relaxation time decreases.

$\text{temperature} \uparrow, \tau \downarrow$

$v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}, \quad V_d \downarrow$

$\sigma = \dfrac{ne^2 \tau}{m}, \quad \sigma \downarrow, \quad \rho \uparrow$

$\mu = \dfrac{e \tau}{m}, \quad \mu \downarrow$

blocks.text:
Series Combination:

$\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{eq}}=\mathrm{R}_1+\mathrm{R}_2+\mathrm{R}_3$

Note:

(a)$\text { In series, I } \rightarrow \text { same }$

(b)$\text { Since } I \text { is same; } V \propto R \text { (As } V=I R)$

(c) For n identical resistances in series:

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{eq}}=\mathrm{nR} \\ & \mathrm{~V}_1=\mathrm{V}_2=\mathrm{V}_3=\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{n}}=\frac{\mathrm{V}_{\text {battery }}}{\mathrm{n}} \end{aligned}$

(d) $\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{eq}}>\left(\mathbf{R}_{\max }\right)_{\text {combination }}$

Parallel Combination :

$\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{eq}}}=\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}_1}+\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}_2}+\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}_3}$

Note:

(a) In parallel V is same across all resistors but current will be different.

(b)$\text { Since } V \text { is same, } I \propto \frac{1}{R}$

(c) In case of 2 resistance  $\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}}=\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}_1}+\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}_2} \Rightarrow \mathrm{R}=\dfrac{\mathrm{R}_1 \mathrm{R}_2}{\mathrm{R}_1+\mathrm{R}_2}$

(d) If n equal resistance are connected in parallel

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{eq}}=\mathrm{R} / \mathrm{n} \\ & \mathrm{I}_1=\mathrm{I}_2=\mathrm{I}_3=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{n}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{total}}}{\mathrm{n}} \end{aligned}$

(e) $\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{eq}}<\left(\mathbf{R}_{\min }\right)_{\text {combination }}$

Concept of Short Circuit : It both terminals of a resistance are connected with a conducting wire then potential of both terminals will become same. In this condition no current will flow through the resistance & we can remove them from the circuit, this is known as short circuit and that resistor is called short circuited or by pass resistor.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Kirchhoff’s First law : This law is also known as junction law or current law (KCL). According to it- In an electric circuit, the algebraic sum of the currents meeting at any junction in the circuit is zero.

Sum of the currents entering the junction is equal to sum of the currents leaving the junction.

This is based on law of conservation of charge.

$\mathrm{i}_1-\mathrm{i}_2-\mathrm{i}_3-\mathrm{i}_4+\mathrm{i}_5=0$

$\mathrm{i}_1+\mathrm{i}_5=\mathrm{i}_2+\mathrm{i}_3+\mathrm{i}_4$

Kirchhoff’s Second law : This law is also known as loop rule or voltage law (KVL) and according to it in any closed circuit the algebraic sum of e.m.f. and algebraic sum of potential drops is zero.

$\Sigma \mathrm{IR}+\Sigma \mathrm{E}=0 .$

In the following closed loop,

$-\mathrm{i}_1 \mathrm{R}_1-\mathrm{i}_1 \mathrm{R}_2-\mathrm{E}_1-\mathrm{i}_4 \mathrm{R}_3+\mathrm{E}_2+\mathrm{E}_3+\mathrm{i}_4 \mathrm{R}_4=0$

Sign Convention for the Applications of Kirchhoff's Second Law

For the application of Kirchhoff's laws, the following sign conventions are to be considered.

• The change in potential in traversing a resistance in the direction of the current is -iR, while in the opposite direction, it is +iR.

Mirror Symmetry

(1) It is applied along perpendicular bisector of line AB (A and B are the points about which Req. is to be calculated).

(2) We can remove resistances and junctions which are on the line of symmetry.

(3) Points on line of symmetry are equipotential points.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Basic Definitions associated with cells and batteries

Symbol of a Cell :

1. EMF(Electromotive Force)(E) : The voltage across the terminals of a cell when it is not delivering any current is called EMF of the cell.

2.Internal Resistance of a Cell(r) : Resistance offered by the electrolyte of the cell when an electric current flows through it is known as internal resistance.

Dependency of internal resistance r is :

  • distance between two electrodes increases$\rightarrow$ r increases
  • Area dipped in electrolyte increases $\rightarrow$r decreases
  • Concentration of electrolyte increases  $\rightarrow$r increases
  • Temperature increases  $\rightarrow$ r decreases
3. Terminal Potential Difference(V) :

• When current is drawn through a cell or current is supplied to it then the potential difference across its terminals is called terminal voltage.

1. During Discharging of a Cell :

The current flows inside the cell from the cathode to the anode.

Current,

$I=\dfrac{E}{R+r}$

$\begin{aligned}
& V_A-E+I r=V_B \\
& V_A-V_B=E-I r
\end{aligned}$

$V=E-I r$

2. When Cell is getting Charged :

Current inside the cell is from anode to cathode.

Current, $I=\dfrac{V-E}{r}$

$\begin{aligned}
& V_A-E+I r=V_B \\
& V_A-V_B=E-I r
\end{aligned}$

During charging the terminal potential difference is greater than the emf of the cell

3. When cell is short circuited :

In short Circuit  $R=0$

$I=\dfrac{E}{R+r}=\dfrac{E}{r} \text { and } V=I R=0$

Note: In short circuit, current from the cell is maximum and terminal potential difference is zero

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Combination of cells in Series and in Parallel

A. Series Combination : When cells are connected in series the total emf of the series combination is equal to the sum of the emf's of the individual cells and the internal resistance of the cells will also be in series.

$\begin{aligned} & E_{e q}=E_1+E_2+E_3+\cdots+E_n \\ & r_{\text {eq }}=r_1+r_2+r_3+\cdots+r_2 \end{aligned}$

B. Parallel Combination :

$\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{eq}}=\dfrac{\dfrac{\mathrm{E}_1}{\mathrm{r}_1}+\dfrac{\mathrm{E}_2}{\mathrm{r}_2}+\dfrac{\mathrm{E}_3}{\mathrm{r}_3}}{\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{r}_1}+\dfrac{1}{r_2}+\dfrac{1}{r_3} \ldots} $

$\quad \dfrac{1}{r_{e q}}=\dfrac{1}{r_1}+\dfrac{1}{r_2}+\dfrac{1}{r_3} \ldots$

When cell support each other

$\begin{aligned} & E_{e q}=\dfrac{E_1 r_2+E_2 r_1}{r_1+r_2} \\ & r_{e q}=\dfrac{r_1+r_2}{r_1+r_2} \end{aligned}$

When cells are connected with opposite polarity

$\begin{aligned} &\text { Let } \mathrm{E}_1>\mathrm{E}_2\\ &\begin{aligned} & E_{e q}=\frac{E_1 r_2-E_2 r_1}{r_1+r_2} \\ & r_{e q}=\frac{r_1 r_2}{r_1+r_2} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$

Note: If n identical cells are connected in parallel and then :-

$\begin{aligned} E_{e q} & =n \dfrac{E / r}{n / r} \\ E_{e q} & =E \\ r_{e q} & =\dfrac{r}{n} \end{aligned}$

Circuit Analysis Involving Combination of Cells

If n identical cells are connected in series and there are m such branches in the circuit then

Total number of cells in this circuit = nm

Internal resistance of the cells connected in a row = nr

total e.m.f. of the cells connected in a row = $E_{\text {net }}$ = nE

Since there are m such rows,

$\text { Total internal resistance of the circuit } \mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{net}}=\frac{\mathrm{nr}}{\mathrm{~m}}$

Total e.m.f. of the circuit = total e.m.f. of the cells connected in a row

$=\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{net}}=\mathrm{nE}$

$\text { Current in the circuit } \mathrm{I}=\dfrac{\mathrm{E}_{\text {net }}}{\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{r}_{\text {net }}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{nE}}{\mathrm{R}+\dfrac{\mathrm{nr}}{\mathrm{~m}}}$

Note : Current I in the circuit is maximum when external resistance in the circuit is equal to the total internal resistance of the cells.

Special case: If in a battery of n identical cells, m cells are wrongly connected. (Consider them is series)

$\text { Number of cells supporting }=(\mathrm{n}-\mathrm{m})$

$\text { Total emf of such cells }=(n-m) E$

$\text { Total emf of cells opposing }=\mathrm{mE}$

$\text { Resultant emf of battery }=(n-m) E-m E=(n-2 m) E$

$\text { Total internal resistance of cells }=\mathrm{nr}$

$\left.\mathrm{E}_{\text {net }}=(\mathrm{n}-2 \mathrm{~m}) \mathrm{E} \quad \text { (Condition } \quad \mathrm{n}>2 \mathrm{~m}\right)$

$I_{n e t}=\dfrac{(n-2 m) E}{R+n r}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Wheatstone Bridge: It is used to find unknown resistance in circuit. None of the shown resistance are in series and none of them are in a parallel.

Balancing condition

$\text { If }\left\{\dfrac{R_1}{R_2}=\dfrac{R_3}{R_4}\right\} $, then bridge is said to be balanced, in this case:

$\begin{aligned} &\left[\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{x}}=\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{y}}\right]\\ &\text { Thus, no current flows in xy branch. } \end{aligned}$

$\dfrac{\mathrm{R}_1}{\mathrm{R}_2}=\dfrac{\mathrm{R}_3}{\mathrm{R}_4} \text { or } \mathrm{R}_1 \mathrm{R}_4=\mathrm{R}_2 \mathrm{R}_3$

Galvanometer : It is used to detect the current i.e. whether current is flowing or not and whether direction of current is reversed or not.

  • Its working is based on torque on current carrying coil. $(\theta \propto i)$
  • Measures small value of current.
  • Maximum value of current at which galvanometer shows maximum deflection or full scale deflection is known as$\text { ' } \mathrm{i}_{\mathrm{g}} \text { ' }$
$\text { Sensitivity = Response/input }$

$\text { (a) Current sensitivity }=\dfrac{\theta}{I}$

$\text { (b) Voltage sensitivity }=\dfrac{\theta}{\mathrm{v}}$

Ammeter:

An ammeter is connected in series with a current carrying wire to measure current passing through it. Since it is connected to the wire and has a finite amount of resistance, there will be some potential difference across it. This will lead to the change in actual flow of current. In an ideal situation where the ammeter can

measure the actual current passing through a wire, there should be no voltage drop across it and hence its resistance should be zero.

Conversion of Galvanometer into Ammeter

• To convert a galvanometer into an ammeter a very small resistance is connected in parallel to the galvanometer called SHUNT.
    • Resistance of an ammeter is very small and it is zero for ideal ammeter i.e. ideal ammeter behaves like conducting wire.
    • Value of shunt.

$\Rightarrow \mathrm{S}=\left[\dfrac{\mathrm{i}_{\mathrm{g}}}{\mathrm{i}-\mathrm{i}_{\mathrm{g}}}\right] \mathrm{G} \Rightarrow \mathrm{~S}=\left[\dfrac{1}{\dfrac{\mathrm{i}}{\mathrm{i}_{\mathrm{g}}}-1}\right] \mathrm{G} \Rightarrow \mathrm{~S}=\left[\dfrac{\mathrm{G}}{\mathrm{n}-1}\right] \text { Where } \mathrm{n}=\dfrac{\mathrm{i}}{\mathrm{i}_{\mathrm{g}}}$

$\text { Where, G - resistance of galvanometer }$

$\mathbf{i}_{\mathrm{g}} $ - range of galvanometer or current required to produce full deflection.

i - Range of ammeter [Max. current can be measured.]$$

Voltmeter :

A voltmeter is connected in parallel to the current carrying wire, to measure the potential difference between two points. Since it is connected to the wire, a finite amount of current will pass through it. This will lead to the change in actual flow of current and hence change in the actual potential difference. In an ideal situation where the voltmeter can measure the actual potential difference across two points, there should be no current passing through it and hence its resistance should be infinite.

Conversion of Galvanometer into Voltmeter:

1. To convert galvanometer into voltmeter, a high resistance is connect in series with a galvanometer.

2. Resistance of voltmeter is very high and it is infinite for ideal voltmeter. so ideal voltmeter ⎯→ open circuit

Resistance R and (G+H) are in parallel between points A and B so we can write

$\mathrm{H}=\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{v}-\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{g}}}{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{g}}}\right) \mathrm{G}=\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{g}}}-1\right) \mathrm{G}$

$\mathrm{H}=(\mathrm{n}-1) \mathrm{G} \quad \text { where } \mathrm{n}=\dfrac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{g}}}$

$\text { V: Range of voltmeter, } \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{g}} \text { : Range of galvanometer }$

Cause of Heating: When current passes through the conductor then drifting electrons transfer their energy to atoms in collisions which increases thermal energy of the conductor, results in increase in temperature. Energy is lost in surroundings in form of heat.

$\mathrm{H}=\mathrm{i}^2 \mathrm{Rt}=\dfrac{\mathrm{V}^2}{\mathrm{R}}=\mathrm{Vit}$

SI unit : joule

Practical Units : 1 kilowatt hour (kWh)

$1 \mathrm{kWh}=3.6 \times 10^6 \text { joules }=1 \text { unit }$

Maximum power transfer theorem

$\text { (a) } P=i^2 R=\left[\dfrac{E}{R+r}\right]^2 R$

If P = max

$\text { Then } \dfrac{\mathrm{dP}}{\mathrm{dR}}=0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{\mathrm{~d}}{\mathrm{dR}}\left[\left[\dfrac{\mathrm{E}}{\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{r}}\right]^2 \mathrm{R}\right]=0$

On solving R = r So, to deliver maximum power to the load resistance. Load resistance should be equal to internal resistance of the cell.

$\text { (b) } i_{P(\max )}=\dfrac{E}{R+R}=\dfrac{E}{2 R}=\dfrac{E}{2 r}$

$\text { where } i_{\mathrm{p}_{(\max )}}=\text { current in case of max. power delivered. }$

$\begin{aligned} & \text { (c) } P_{(\max )}=\left[\frac{E}{2 R}\right]^2 R \\ & P_{(\max )}=\frac{E^2}{4 R}=\frac{E^2}{4 r} \end{aligned}$

Resistance of an electrical device

$\begin{aligned} & R=\frac{V_S^2}{P_S}=\frac{V_A^2}{P_C} \Rightarrow \frac{V_S^2}{P_S}=\frac{V_A^2}{P_C} \\ & \text { Hence } P_C=\left(\frac{V_A}{V_S}\right) P_S \end{aligned}$

$\text { As } \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{s}}=\text { constant } \Rightarrow \mathrm{R} \propto \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{s}}}$

$P_S \uparrow, R \downarrow \text {, thickness of filament } \uparrow$

$\text { For example : } \mathrm{R}_{40 \mathrm{~W}}>\mathrm{R}_{100 \mathrm{W}}$

Combination of bulbs

(a) Series combination

$\begin{aligned} & R=R_1+R_2 \\ & \frac{V^2}{P}=\frac{V_1^2}{P_1}+\frac{V_2^2}{P_2} \end{aligned}$

(When rated voltage is not given, take it equal to applied voltage.)

$\begin{aligned} &\frac{1}{\mathrm{P}}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{P}_1}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{P}_2}\\ &\text { In case of } \mathrm{n} \text {-identical bulbs }\\ &P_{\text {series }}=\frac{P}{n} \end{aligned}$

Note:

$\text { Brightness } \propto \text { Power consumed by bulb } \propto \mathrm{R} \propto \frac{1}{\mathrm{P}_{\text {rated }}} \text {. }$

Bulb of lesser wattage will shine more.

$\text { For same current } P=I^2 R \quad \text { so } \quad P \propto R \Rightarrow R \uparrow, P \uparrow$

(b) Parallel combination

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{R}=\frac{1}{R_1}+\frac{1}{R_2} \\ & \frac{P}{V_S^2}=\frac{P_1}{V_s^2}+\frac{P_2}{V_S^2} \\ & P=P_1+P_2 \end{aligned}$

In case of n-identical bulbs

$\mathrm{P}_{\text {parallel }}=\mathrm{nP}$

Note:

Brightness $ \propto \text { power consumed by bulb } \propto \frac{1}{\mathrm{R}} \propto \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{s}}$

Bulb of greater wattage will shine more.

For same V,  P = $\frac{\mathrm{V}^2}{\mathrm{R}} $  more power will be consumed in smaller resistance P $\propto$ $\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}}$

Let two coil boil some amount of water in times  $\mathrm{t}_1 \text { and } \mathrm{t}_2$ separately Now these coils are connected in series and then parallel then time required to boil same amount of water.

In series combination

$\begin{aligned} &\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{\mathrm{P}}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{P}_1}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{P}_2} \\ & \frac{\mathrm{t}}{\mathrm{H}}=\frac{\mathrm{t}_1}{\mathrm{H}}+\frac{\mathrm{t}_2}{\mathrm{H}} \end{aligned}\\ &\mathrm{t}=\mathrm{t}_1+\mathrm{t}_2 \end{aligned}$

In parallel combination

$\begin{aligned} & P=P_1+P_2 \\ & \frac{H}{t}=\frac{H}{t_1}+\frac{H}{t_2} \\ & \frac{1}{t}=\frac{1}{t_1}+\frac{1}{t_2} \Rightarrow t=\frac{t_1 t_2}{t_1+t_2} \end{aligned}$

NOTE: Instruments based on heating effects of current, work with both A.C. and D.C. Equal values of A.C. (RMS) and D.C. produce equal heating effect. Due to this reason, the brightness of bulb is same whether it is operated by A.C. or an equivalent D.C.
